Body HTML:
TOTO toilets, toilet parts, seats, urinals and sinks. This collection leans toward repair and replacement: bowls and tanks sold as separate part numbers, fill valves, flappers, trip levers, tank-to-bowl gaskets and SoftClose seats, alongside one-piece toilets, wall-hung bowls and the DuoFit in-wall tank systems they mount on. Commercial items include urinals and flush valves. Many bowls carry CEFIONTECT, TOTO's ceramic glaze, and some tanks are built for a WASHLET+ bidet seat connection. Most china is listed in Cotton White (#01); the color code is a suffix on the part number, so #01 and #12 of the same model are the same fixture in different colors. When you are replacing half of a two-piece toilet, work from the part number on the piece you still have, because TOTO pairs specific bowls with specific tanks.

How to choose

  • Bowl and tank: a two-piece TOTO is two part numbers. Match the bowl and tank by model, not by series name alone.
  • Rough-in: measure from the finished wall to the center of the closet flange bolts. On bowls that use it, the UniFit adapter sets a 10", 12" or 14" rough-in.
  • Wall-hung: a TOTO wall-hung bowl mounts on a DuoFit in-wall tank system with dual flush at 1.28 and 0.9 GPF. The push plate is ordered separately from the tank unit.
  • Flush valve size: many TOTO tanks use a 3" flush valve and some older models use a 2" valve. The flapper has to match.
  • Commercial spud: urinals and flushometer bowls come with a top spud or back spud. The position is not adjustable, so match it to the existing supply.

TOTO lines and part numbers

Bowls and tanks are separate part numbers. Thirty-six items here are listed as bowl only and twenty as tank only. A two-piece Toto is two orders. When you are replacing half of an existing toilet, work from the part number cast or printed on the piece you still have — Toto pairs specific bowls with specific tanks, and a model name alone will not tell you which.

UniFit sets the rough-in. For the toilets that use it, the UniFit outlet adapter is what decides whether the bowl lands on your waste line: TSU08W.10, TSU08W.12 and TSU08W.14 give 10", 12" and 14" rough-in from the same bowl. Measure from the finished wall — not the baseboard — to the center of the closet flange bolts before ordering.

DuoFit is the in-wall system. Ten items are DuoFit: in-wall dual-flush tank units at 1.28 and 0.9 GPF with copper supply, plus the push-button plates that finish them. Plates come round and rectangular in matte silver, matte white and stainless, and are ordered separately from the tank unit — the tank goes in during rough-in, the plate after the wall is closed.

Commercial. Five urinals, including washout models with top spud and back spud and two at 0.125 GPF; four urinal flush valves and four toilet flush valves. Spud position is not adjustable, so match it to the existing supply before ordering. Eight items are identified as ADA compliant.

WASHLET and glaze. Thirty-seven items reference WASHLET, Toto's bidet seat line, including WASHLET+ auto-flush-ready tank units. Thirty-four carry CEFIONTECT, Toto's ceramic glaze.

Finishes. Ninety-six items are Cotton White (#01) and sixteen are polished chrome. Toto's color codes are suffixes on the part number, so #01 and #12 of the same model are the same fixture in different colors.

Popular in this collection: TOTO TSU99A.XR Adjustable Fill Valve, TOTO THU500S 3" Replacement Flapper, TOTO SS114#01 SoftClose Elongated Seat, TOTO Drake ST776EA#01 Toilet Tank.

Common questions

Which TOTO flapper do I need?

Match the flapper to the flush valve in the tank. Many TOTO tanks use a 3" flush valve, which takes flappers such as the THU500S, and some older models use a 2" valve. Check the tank model number, printed inside the tank.

Will a TOTO fill valve fit any toilet?

The TSU99A.XR is an adjustable fill valve made for TOTO tanks. Set its height to the tank as described in the instructions, so the water level sits at the mark inside the tank.

Elongated or round TOTO seat?

Measure from the seat bolt holes to the front edge of the bowl: about 18-1/2" is elongated and about 16-1/2" is round. TOTO SoftClose seats are made in both shapes.

Wall-hung toilet bowls and in-wall tank systems from Duravit, TOTO and Zurn. Duravit models include Starck 3, ME by Starck, Darling New and Happy D.2 in elongated, round and compact shapes, many of them rimless and ADA compliant, with dual flush at 1.28/0.8 or 1.6/0.8 GPF. TOTO wall-hung toilets here are the RP and SP bowls with CEFIONTECT glaze and dual flush at 1.28 and 0.9 GPF, along with the TOTO DuoFit in-wall tank systems they mount on. The Zurn Z5615 is a top spud siphon-jet bowl for a flush valve rather than a concealed tank. A wall-hung toilet carries no weight on the floor: the bowl bolts to a carrier inside the wall and the tank sits in the wall cavity, so the wall hung toilet carrier and tank are chosen before the wall is closed.

How to choose

  • Carrier and tank system: a wall-mount bowl needs a compatible in-wall carrier and concealed tank. Confirm which system the bowl is designed for before ordering; TOTO bowls pair with DuoFit tanks.
  • Flush volume: dual flush at 1.28/0.8, 1.6/0.8 or 1.28 and 0.9 GPF. Check the flush volume against local requirements.
  • Bowl shape and projection: elongated, round or compact elongated. Check the projection from the wall for clearances; Duravit Starck 3 is listed at 21-1/4" and 24-3/8".
  • Rim height: the carrier sets the bowl height, which is how ADA rim heights are reached.
  • What is included: check whether the seat and actuator plate are included or ordered separately, and whether the bowl is for a concealed tank or a top spud flush valve.

Common questions

What do I need to install a wall-mount toilet?

An in-wall carrier and concealed tank made for that bowl, plus the actuator plate and seat if they are not included. Confirm the carrier system before ordering the bowl.

Can the bowl height be adjusted?

Yes. On a wall-hung toilet the carrier sets the bowl height, which is how ADA rim heights are reached.

Do wall-mount toilets save space?

They free up floor space and make cleaning under the bowl easy, while the tank sits inside the wall cavity.

Body HTML:
Toilet bowls sold separately from the tank, for two-piece installations, wall-hung carriers and commercial flushometer applications, from American Standard, TOTO, Gerber, Duravit and DXV. Most are elongated, and round front bowls cover tight rooms. The range includes chair height bowls (also called comfort height or right height) and ADA bowls, skirted bowls with a concealed trapway, wall-hung bowls that mount on an in-wall carrier, floor-mount flushometer bowls with a top or back spud, and pressure assist bowls that work only with a pressure assist tank. American Standard bowls with EverClean and TOTO bowls with CEFIONTECT glaze are listed, and a few ship with a seat. A bowl and its tank are engineered as a set, so buy both from the same model family, or match the model number on the piece you are keeping. The matching toilet tanks are on their own page.

How to choose

  • Rough-in: the distance from the finished wall to the centerline of the closet bolts. 12" is standard; 10" and 14" exist in older construction. Check the model's spec sheet when the title does not state it.
  • Bowl shape: elongated runs about two inches longer front to back; round front saves that space in a small room.
  • Bowl height: standard height is about 14-1/2" to 15" at the rim; chair height is roughly 16-1/2" to 18". ADA asks for a seat top between 17" and 19".
  • Type: tank-type, wall-hung or flushometer. Flushometer bowls take a top spud or back spud, and the two are not interchangeable.
  • Tank match: flush volume, trapway and tank outlet are designed together. Pressure assist bowls need a pressure assist tank.

Elongated or round front

An elongated toilet bowl runs about two inches longer front to back and is the more comfortable of the two, which is why 83 of the bowls here are elongated. Round front - 16 of them - buys those two inches back, and that matters more often than people expect: a door that swings into the fixture, a vanity opposite, a powder room where the code clearance in front of the bowl is already tight. Measure the space in front of the flange before you decide on comfort.

Chair height, comfort height and right height are the same thing

Three names, one specification. All of them mean a bowl whose rim sits roughly 16-1/2 to 18 inches off the floor instead of the traditional 14-1/2 to 15. Twenty-four bowls here are called out as chair or right height. Standing up off one is easier on knees and hips, which is the whole point - and it is also why it has quietly become the default in new residential work.

One measurement detail people get wrong: the height that matters is to the top of the seat, not the rim. A seat adds roughly half an inch to an inch, so a 17-inch rim and a thick seat can land above the range you were aiming for.

What ADA actually requires

Thirteen bowls here are specifically called out as ADA, including American Standard's Afwall ADA Retrofit. It is worth being precise about what that means, because the bowl is only one input. The standard asks for a seat top between 17 and 19 inches, clear floor space beside and in front of the fixture, a flush control on the open side of the approach, and an operating force that a closed fist can manage. A chair height bowl makes compliance possible; the installation, the seat and the flush control decide whether you get there. If you are specifying for a commercial job, work from the drawing, not from the product page.

Rough-in: check it, and know where to find it

Rough-in is the distance from the finished wall to the centerline of the closet bolts. Twelve inches is standard; 10" and 14" exist in older construction, and a bowl for the wrong rough-in will not sit against the wall.

Being straight about a gap in our own listings: only one of these 106 states the rough-in in the title. Work from the model number, or from the manufacturer's spec sheet for that model. And if the flange is in the wrong place and moving the drain is not realistic, the TOTO Unifit adapters convert a single bowl between 10", 12" and 14" - that is exactly the problem they exist to solve.

Three different machines: tank-type, wall-hung and flushometer

Eighty-nine of these are conventional tank-type bowls for a two-piece toilet. Ten are wall-hung, which carry no weight on the floor and need a carrier inside the wall - the Geberit and Grohe in-wall carriers are with the toilet repair parts. Seven are floor-mount flushometer bowls with no tank connection at all: they take a spud and a flush valve fed straight off the supply, which is why you see them in schools and offices where a tank could not refill fast enough between uses.

Thirteen bowls carry a spud - ten top spud, three back spud - and the two are not interchangeable. Top spud takes the flush valve above the bowl; back spud takes it behind, through the wall. Match it to the valve and the wall penetration you already have.

Skirted bowls and EverClean

Ten of these are skirted: the trapway is concealed behind a smooth outer wall instead of the usual molded contour. The reason is cleaning - there is no channel behind the bowl to reach into. The trade-off is that skirted bowls usually mount with a bracket system rather than plain closet bolts, so read the install instructions before you assume it drops onto the existing flange. Thirteen bowls carry American Standard's EverClean glaze, and seven ship with a seat included.

Match the bowl to the tank

Four of these are pressure assist bowls, which only work with a pressure assist tank - the vessel is in the tank, and the bowl's trapway is sized for that discharge. The same logic holds more generally: flush volume, trapway and tank outlet are engineered as a set. Buy the bowl and the tank from the same model family, and if you are replacing only one half, match the model number on the piece you are keeping.

Common questions

Can I buy a toilet bowl without the tank?

Yes. On a two-piece toilet the bowl and tank are separate part numbers. The bowl has to match the tank from the same model family, so check the model number on the tank you are keeping.

Is chair height the same as comfort height?

Yes. Chair height, comfort height and right height all describe a bowl whose rim sits roughly 16-1/2" to 18" off the floor instead of the traditional 14-1/2" to 15".

How do I measure toilet rough-in?

Measure from the finished wall, not the baseboard, to the center of the closet bolts. 12" is standard, and 10" and 14" are found in older construction.

Body HTML:
Replacement toilet tanks sold on their own, without a bowl, from American Standard, TOTO, Gerber, Duravit and DXV. A two-piece toilet is a matched pair: the tank's outlet, bolt pattern, flush valve height and water volume are designed around one specific bowl, so a replacement tank has to come from the correct model family. Tanks here are built for 10-inch, 12-inch and 14-inch rough-in and flush at 1.0, 1.1, 1.28 or 1.6 gpf. The range includes dual flush tanks, American Standard pressure assist tanks, lined tanks that resist condensation, right-hand and left-hand trip lever versions, TOTO tanks compatible with WASHLET+, and colors beyond white such as Bone, Linen and Colonial White. Find the model number inside your existing tank, usually on the back wall above the water line or under the lid, and match it. The toilet bowls are on their own page.

How to choose

  • Model match: a tank is not a universal part. Match the model number cast or printed inside the existing tank, or the model of the bowl.
  • Rough-in: 12" is the modern standard; 10" and 14" tanks are made for specific bowls. Many titles state the rough-in.
  • Flush volume: 1.28 gpf, 1.6 gpf, or 1.0 and 1.1 gpf high-efficiency. Match what the bowl was built for.
  • Trip lever hand: left-hand is the usual position; right-hand versions are listed for toilets in a corner or beside a vanity.
  • Gravity or pressure assist: pressure assist tanks hold a sealed vessel and pair only with pressure assist bowls.

A toilet tank is not a universal part

This is the one thing worth getting right before anything else. A two-piece toilet is engineered as a matched pair: the tank's outlet, its bolt pattern, its flush valve height and its water volume are all designed around one specific bowl. A replacement toilet tank from the correct model family will bolt down and flush properly. One that merely looks similar will either not seat on the bolt holes, or will seat and then flush badly forever. Find the model number cast inside your existing tank - usually on the back wall above the water line, or under the lid - and match it.

Rough-in: 10, 12 or 14 inches

Rough-in is the distance from the finished wall to the center of the closet flange bolts. Twelve inches is the modern standard and covers 36 of the tanks here; 6 are built for a 10-inch rough-in, common in houses built before the 1960s and in some compact bathrooms, and one is 14-inch. The Duravit DuraSystem WD1022000091 is different again - an in-wall carrier tank that hides inside a 2x4 or 2x6 stud bay.

Forty-four of these carry the rough-in in the product title. For the other 34 - most of the TOTO range among them - check the specification block further down the product page, where it often appears. Where it is not listed at all, work from the bowl's model number rather than from a tape measure, because the manufacturer pairs the tank to a named bowl rather than to a dimension.

Flush volume has to match the bowl

Forty-eight of these are 1.28 gpf, the usual high-efficiency volume for a new toilet; 15 are 1.6 gpf for older bowls designed around that volume; a handful are 1.0 and 1.1 gpf high-efficiency. Putting a 1.28 gpf tank on a bowl engineered for 1.6 gpf does not save water - it starves a trapway sized for more, and you get double flushes, which uses more. Match what the bowl was built for.

Dual flush and pressure assist

Eight tanks are dual flush: a full flush for solids and a reduced one for liquids, either through a split trip lever or a top push button. The TOTO Aquia IV family and Duravit's DuraStyle and ME by Starck use the button.

Four American Standard tanks are pressure assist, and these are a different machine entirely. Inside the china tank sits a sealed plastic vessel. Incoming line pressure compresses air above the water, and the flush releases that stored pressure rather than relying on gravity and head height. The result is a forceful, short, loud flush that clears a bowl in one go - which is why they are standard in commercial restrooms. None of the internal parts interchange with a gravity tank, and they need a minimum of about 20 psi of static line pressure to work.

Trip lever hand and WASHLET+ routing

Thirteen of these have a right-hand trip lever and five are explicitly left-hand; the rest are standard left. It sounds trivial until the toilet sits in a corner or beside a vanity and the handle is against the wall. Separately, twelve TOTO tanks are WASHLET+ compatible, which means the tank is built to route the supply line to a bidet seat through a concealed connection rather than a visible tee - a detail that only matters if you are installing a WASHLET, and matters a lot if you are.

Lined tanks and colors

American Standard's "Lined" tanks (4188A054, 4188A154 and 4425A154) carry a foam liner bonded to the inside of the china. In a humid bathroom, cold supply water chills the tank wall below the dew point and it sweats - the puddle on the floor that looks like a leak but is not. The liner stops it. Ten tanks here come in something other than plain white: Bone, Linen, Sedona Beige, Colonial White, Canvas White and Ebony.

What else the job needs

A tank swap is rarely just the tank. You will want the tank-to-bowl gasket and bolt set, and a new flush valve and fill valve if the old ones are anything but new - see toilet repair parts. If the toilet is coming off the floor, add a wax ring and closet bolts. And while the water is off, it is the right moment to replace the angle stop and the toilet supply line.

Common questions

Are toilet tanks universal?

No. The tank outlet, bolt pattern, flush valve height and water volume are designed around a specific bowl. Order the tank from the same model family as the bowl.

Where is the model number on a toilet tank?

It is usually cast or stamped inside the tank on the back wall above the water line, or under the lid.

Can I put a 1.28 gpf tank on a 1.6 gpf bowl?

It is not a good match. A bowl designed for 1.6 gpf has a trapway sized for that volume, and a smaller flush can leave it needing a second flush. Match the tank to the bowl model.

Toilet seats from TOTO, Bemis, Duravit, American Standard and DXV: round and elongated, closed front and open front, in plastic and enameled wood, plus electronic bidet seats. About half are soft-close or slow-close, where the lid and ring lower under damping instead of slamming; TOTO calls it SoftClose, while Duravit and American Standard call it slow-close. Open-front seats from TOTO, Bemis and American Standard are made for public and employee restrooms, most of them heavy duty. Bemis names the hinge and mounting system in the model: self-sustaining or non-self-sustaining check hinges, and STA-TITE or Top-Tite mounting that keeps the seat from shifting. Electronic bidet seats include TOTO WASHLET models, the DXV AT100 SpaLet and Duravit SensoWash. Seat shape is measured on the bowl, not the seat, so measure before ordering.

How to choose

  • Bowl shape: measure from the center of the two bolt holes to the outside front edge of the bowl. About 16-1/2" is round; about 18-1/2" is elongated.
  • Open or closed front: public and employee restrooms generally call for an open-front seat; local code settles which version applies. Closed front is the usual residential style.
  • Hinge and mounting: soft-close, self-sustaining or standard hinges; lift-off and telescoping models release without tools for cleaning.
  • Material: plastic (polypropylene on most) is light and easy to sanitize; enameled wood is heavier.
  • Bidet seats: electronic seats need power at the toilet. WASHLET+ models pair with specific TOTO bowls, so check the bowl first.

Toilet seat types in detail

Round or elongated is the first thing to get right, and it is measured on the bowl, not the seat. Take the distance from the center of the two bolt holes at the back to the outside front edge of the china. Round comes out around 16-1/2"; elongated around 18-1/2". The seats stocked here bear that out — the round ones run 16-5/16" to 16-7/8" front to back and the elongated run 18-7/16" to 19-1/16". A seat one size off will bolt down and still overhang or undercut the rim, and it is the single most common reason a seat goes back in the box.

Open front is a code requirement, not a style. Public and employee restrooms generally call for an open-front seat, with or without a cover depending on the occupancy — the split in the bowl-front is there so the seat is not contacted where it matters. 13 open-front seats are stocked, from Toto, Bemis and American Standard, most of them heavy duty for commercial traffic. A closed-front residential seat in a public restroom is a failed inspection, and the local code is what settles which version applies.

The hinge is what wears out, not the seat. Bemis names the mechanism in the model: a self-sustaining check hinge holds the seat and lid wherever they are left, which is what a commercial spec usually calls for; a non-self-sustaining hinge lets them fall. STA-TITE and Top-Tite are the mounting systems — they clamp the seat so it stops shifting side to side, which is the failure that makes a good seat feel cheap after a year. Where the seat has to come off for cleaning, the telescoping and lift-off models release without tools.

32 of these are soft-close or slow-close: the lid and ring drop under damping instead of slamming, which saves the hinge, the china and the household. Toto calls it SoftClose, Duravit and American Standard call it slow-close, and the mechanism does the same job.

Material splits three ways. Plastic — polypropylene on most of these — is light, easy to sanitize and the standard for commercial. Enameled wood is heavier and warmer to sit on, and three are stocked in that construction from Bemis. Toto’s EverClean and comparable surfaces add a glaze that resists staining on high-traffic bowls.

Electronic bidet seats are the other category here entirely. Nine are stocked — Toto WASHLET (S7A, S7, K300, A2 and a WASHLET+ Ready square), the DXV AT100 SpaLet and two Duravit SensoWash, one of them with remote and app control. All of them need power at the toilet, which means a GFCI receptacle within reach of the cord and usually an electrician before the plumber. The WASHLET+ models are built to pair with specific Toto bowls that route the supply and cord out of sight — check the bowl before ordering the seat, because the concealed connection only works on the matched pairing.

Common questions

How do I know if I need a round or elongated seat?

Measure the bowl from the center of the two bolt holes to the front edge of the rim. About 16-1/2" is round and about 18-1/2" is elongated.

Do electronic bidet seats need an outlet?

Yes. They need power at the toilet, usually a GFCI receptacle within reach of the cord, and a water connection at the toilet supply.

What is the difference between open-front and closed-front seats?

Open-front seats have a gap at the front and are common in public and commercial restrooms, where codes often require them. Closed-front seats are the usual residential style.

Body HTML:
Toilet repair parts: fill valves, flappers, flush valves, trip levers and push-button actuators, tank-to-bowl kits and gaskets, rough-in adapters, flange spacers and shims, from TOTO, Fluidmaster, Pasco, Sioux Chief, American Standard, Duravit, Geberit and Oatey. Most toilet problems trace to two parts. A toilet that runs, with water trickling into the bowl or the tank refilling on its own, is usually the flapper. A toilet that refills slowly, overfills into the overflow tube or hammers when it shuts off is usually the fill valve. Universal parts such as the Fluidmaster 400A fill valve fit most two-piece toilets, while TOTO and American Standard parts are matched to the toilet model. Check the model number printed inside the tank and measure the flush valve opening, 2 inches or 3 inches, before ordering.

How to choose

  • Flapper size: measure the opening in the tank bottom, 2" or 3". A 2" flapper will not seal a 3" valve.
  • Universal or model-specific: many fill valves are universal; flappers, canister seals and gaskets for TOTO and American Standard are often matched to the toilet model.
  • Trip lever mount: front, left-side and right-side mount are separate parts, and finish matters because the lever is visible.
  • Tank-to-bowl kit: bolt spacing and gasket diameter follow the manufacturer, so choose the kit made for the toilet brand.
  • In-wall tanks: concealed tanks from TOTO, Duravit, Geberit and Grohe take their own actuator plates and fill valve parts.

Which part do I need?

  • Toilet runs or refills by itself: replace the flapper. Measure the opening in the tank bottom first, 2" or 3".
  • Tank fills slowly, overfills or hisses: replace the fill valve. Universal fill valves fit most two-piece toilets.
  • New flapper still leaks: the flush valve seat is worn. Replace the flush valve or use a seat repair kit.
  • Handle is loose or will not lift the flapper: replace the trip lever (front, left or right mount).
  • Water drips between the tank and bowl: fit a tank-to-bowl kit made for your toilet brand.
  • Leak or rocking at the floor: replace the wax ring and closet bolts, see wax rings and bolts.
  • Commercial toilet with a flushometer (no tank): see flush valve parts and repair kits or a new toilet flush valve.

A cracked tank or bowl cannot be repaired with parts: see replacement toilet tanks, toilet bowls or complete toilets.

Diagnose it before you buy

Almost every toilet complaint is one of two parts. A toilet that runs - water trickling into the bowl, the tank refilling every few minutes with nobody in the room - is nearly always the flapper. A toilet that refills slowly, overfills into the overflow tube, or hammers when it shuts off is nearly always the fill valve. They age together, so many repairs replace both at once.

Flapper size is the first thing to check

Two-inch and three-inch flush valves are both common, they look identical in a photograph, and a 2" toilet flapper on a 3" valve will not seal at all. Measure the opening in the bottom of the tank before ordering - not the flapper you pulled out, which may itself have been the wrong part.

Fluidmaster's PRO53, PRO54 and PRO55 are universal-fit flappers; the PRO56 and the 502P21 Adjust-A-Flush are adjustable, which lets you tune how long the flapper stays open and therefore how much water each flush uses. The PRO58 is the 3" adjustable. Pasco's 22001 and 22054 are the plain 2" trade flappers. TOTO's THU500S fits their 3" tanks, and the THU227 is the Aquia dual-flush seal, sold ten to a pack.

One thing that kills flappers: in-tank chlorine tablets. The rubber goes hard and glazed in months instead of years. If the flapper you removed feels like a hockey puck, that is why.

Fill valves

The Fluidmaster 400A is the part most American toilets end up with eventually - a universal anti-siphon toilet fill valve that adjusts for height. The 400LS adds Leak Sentry, which shuts the valve if the flapper leaks. The PRO45, PRO45B and PRO45K are the contractor-grade versions, and the K is the kit with the shank washer and refill tube. American Standard's 7381125-400 and TOTO's TSU99A.XR are the manufacturer equivalents. TOTO's Geberit-style concealed tanks take their own filling-valve nipple and fixation clip.

Set the water level to the mark molded into the overflow tube - usually about an inch below its top. Higher and the tank simply drains into the overflow forever; lower and the flush is weak.

Flush valve is not the same as the flapper

The flapper is the rubber seal. The flush valve is the whole seat-and-overflow assembly it sits on, and it only needs replacing when the seat itself is pitted or cracked - run a fingertip around it, and if it catches, no new flapper will seal. Fluidmaster's 507AP7, PRO57 and PRO57K cover the common sizes; the 555CRP8 Flusher Fixer Kit bonds a new seat over the old one without pulling the tank, which is the repair to reach for when the tank bolts are corroded.

Trip levers are handed, and the nut is reverse-threaded

Front, left-side and right-side mount are separate parts - check which one you have before ordering. And the trip lever nut is left-hand threaded on most brands: it tightens counterclockwise. This catches people constantly, because the instinct when it will not loosen is to pull harder in the direction that is actually tightening it.

Levers are visible, so finish matters: chrome, brushed nickel, polished nickel, matte black, platinum, cotton white and ebony are all stocked. TOTO's THU068 fits Drake tanks except the R-suffix models, which is the kind of detail worth reading twice. For in-wall tanks, six TOTO DuoFit push-button plates and the Duravit, Geberit, Grohe and DXV actuator plates replace the lever entirely.

Tank-to-bowl kits are brand-specific

The bolts, washers and sponge gasket between tank and bowl are not universal - the bolt spacing and the gasket diameter follow the manufacturer. Sioux Chief stocks six kits by brand: American Standard, Gerber, Kohler (two versions), Eljer and Mansfield. American Standard has its own EZ Install kits, and TOTO's gaskets are called out per toilet model rather than per size. If you are pulling a tank, replace the gasket and bolts - they are the usual reason the tank leaks at the base.

Unifit adapters change a toilet's rough-in

Seven TOTO Unifit trapway adapters let one bowl serve a 10", 12" or 14" rough-in. This is genuinely useful in a remodel where the flange is not where the new toilet expects it: instead of moving the drain, you fit the matching adapter. TSU01W covers CT474, MS614 and MS644; TSU03W the 934, 964 and 974 one-piece toilets; TSU08W the Aquia IV. See replacement toilet tanks for the rough-in question from the tank side.

Flange spacers, shims and Liquilock

When the finished floor went in over the old one, the closet flange ends up below the tile and the bowl rocks. Oatey's 43412 and 43413 flange spacers (1/4" and 1/8") and the Pasco 1018 extension bring it back up; Sioux Chief's Wedge-It shims level the bowl without shimming with coins. And Oatey Liquilock is the one nobody knows about - a gel that turns the water in the bowl and trap solid so you can lift the toilet without it running down the hallway. It liquefies again with water.

Popular in this collection: Toto 9BU024E 3" Tank to Bowl Gasket, TOTO YT920#MS Dual Flush Push Plate.

Common questions

Why does my toilet keep running?

A running toilet is almost always the flapper or the fill valve. Put a few drops of food coloring in the tank: if color reaches the bowl without flushing, the flapper or flush valve seal is leaking. If the water level rises into the overflow tube, the fill valve needs adjusting or replacing.

Do I need a 2-inch or 3-inch flapper?

Match the flush valve opening in the tank. Many older toilets use 2-inch valves and many newer high-efficiency toilets use 3-inch valves, so check the toilet model or measure the drain opening.

Are toilet repair parts universal?

Many fill valves are universal, but flush valves, flappers, canister seals and tank-to-bowl gaskets for brands like TOTO and American Standard are often model-specific. Match the part to the toilet model number printed inside the tank.

Alcove bathtubs from Maax, Duravit, American Standard, Bootz and Mustee in acrylic, Americast, porcelain-enameled steel and molded fiberglass, in white and linen. An alcove tub is built for a three-wall recess: the front is finished with an integral apron, and the other sides are unfinished because they disappear into the framing. Most alcove tubs here are 60 inches long and 30 or 32 inches wide, with 54-inch, 66-inch and 72-inch models for other openings. Each is listed with a left-hand or right-hand drain, and the Maax line adds end-drain and center-drain models. Maax Rubix and Exhibit tubs are also listed in AFR (above-the-floor rough) versions. Whatever the material, an alcove tub needs a properly bedded, level base: a tub set on an uneven floor flexes and can crack at the apron.

How to choose

  • Size: measure the framed opening. 60" x 30" and 60" x 32" are the common sizes here; 54", 66" and 72" tubs are listed for other openings.
  • Drain hand: standing at the open face of the alcove, a right-hand drain tub drains at your right. This cannot be corrected on site.
  • Material: acrylic is light and warm to the touch; enameled steel is harder and more scratch-resistant but conducts heat away; Americast is American Standard's enameled steel material.
  • Rough-in type: AFR models are made for an above-the-floor drain rough-in. Check the model against how the waste is run.
  • Drain: the waste and overflow is usually a separate item; Duravit listings state "drain sold separately".

Shop alcove tubs by brand

  • Maax (acrylic): Rubix 6030, Rubix 6032, Rubix 6632, Exhibit 6030, Exhibit 6032, Exhibit 6036, Exhibit 6636, Exhibit 7236, Tempest 60 x 36 and VO6042 AcrylX.

  • Bootz (porcelain-enameled steel): 60" x 30" left drain, 60" x 30" right drain and the 54" Kona 5430.
  • Mustee (molded fiberglass): 60" x 30" left drain and right drain.

Alcove tubs by material

  • Acrylic alcove tubs: Maax Rubix, Exhibit, Tempest and VO6042, and Duravit No.1 and Architec. Light to carry and warm to the touch.
  • Porcelain and enameled steel: the Bootz porcelain-enameled steel tubs, plus American Standard Princeton and Cambridge in Americast, American Standard's enameled steel material.
  • Fiberglass: the Mustee one-piece molded tubs.

Alcove tubs by size and drain side

  • 54" tubs: Bootz Kona 5430 left hand and right hand.
  • 5 ft (60") tubs: the standard alcove size, in 30", 32" and 36" depths from the brands above, plus the 42" deep Maax VO6042.

  • Left-hand drain alcove tubs: American Standard Studio, American Standard Princeton, Maax Rubix 6032, Duravit No.1 and Bootz 60" x 30". Most models above come in both hands.

Common questions

How do I tell a left-hand from a right-hand drain tub?

Stand at the open face of the alcove and look at the tub. If the drain is at your left, it is a left-hand drain; at your right, a right-hand drain. Order the hand that matches the waste rough-in.

What size is an alcove tub?

Most alcove tubs here are 60" long and 30" or 32" wide. Bootz Kona is 54" long, and Maax lists 66" and 72" models. Measure the framed opening before ordering.

Acrylic or enameled steel?

Acrylic is light to carry, warm to the touch and holds bath temperature. Porcelain-enameled steel is harder and more scratch-resistant but conducts heat away, so it is often insulated.

Pipe escutcheons and floor and ceiling plates: the trim rings that cover the opening where a pipe passes through a wall, floor or ceiling. Most of this collection is Pasco: Sure Grip flanges, box flanges, low flanges and floor and ceiling plates in solid and split styles, in chrome and white. Sioux Chief adds shallow flange and split plastic escutcheons, and Dearborn a cast brass flange with a set screw. Sizes follow the pipe, from 1/2 inch upward, in both CTS (copper tube size, shown as CWT in Pasco titles) and IPS (iron pipe size). A few fixture-specific pieces are also here, including Moen, Grohe and Delta shower and faucet escutcheons and a Sioux Chief tub spout seal. In a fire-rated assembly an escutcheon is cosmetic only; the penetration still needs a listed firestop behind it.

How to choose

  • Pipe standard: CTS and IPS escutcheons of the same nominal size have different bores and are not interchangeable. Identify the pipe first.
  • Depth: a shallow escutcheon sits nearly flat and covers a neat hole; a deep or box flange has a raised skirt that covers a ragged or oversized opening.
  • Solid or split: split (hinged) versions go on pipe that is already installed, without breaking a joint.
  • Opening size: on a retrofit, measure the actual opening so the plate covers it.
  • Finish: chrome and white are the usual choices; match the stop or the wall.

Common questions

What size escutcheon do I need?

Match the nominal pipe size and the pipe standard. A 1/2" CTS escutcheon fits 1/2" copper tube, and a 1/2" IPS escutcheon fits 1/2" iron pipe size; the bores are different.

What is a split escutcheon?

A split or hinged escutcheon opens to fit around pipe that is already installed, so the trim can go on without breaking a joint.

What is a floor and ceiling plate?

It does the same job as an escutcheon on vertical risers, covering the opening where the pipe passes through a floor or ceiling.

Widespread bathroom faucets from Delta, Moen, hansgrohe, Grohe, Brizo, American Standard, Pfister and Gerber. A widespread faucet has a separate spout and two handles mounted in three holes, typically 8 inches apart from handle to handle. Moen widespread faucets include the Align, Brantford, Eva, Gibson, Glyde, Voss and Greenfield lines; several are sold as trim kits that mount on a separate Moen rough-in valve, and the listing title says whether the valve is included. Delta lines include Trinsic, Ashlyn and Nicoli, and American Standard adds Edgemere and Townsend. Finishes include chrome, brushed nickel, polished nickel, oil rubbed bronze and matte black. An Elkay 8-inch commercial deck-mount faucet is also listed. Check the sink or countertop drilling, the spout reach over the bowl and whether a drain assembly is included before ordering.

How to choose

  • Hole spacing: three holes, typically 8" from handle to handle. Measure the sink or countertop drilling.
  • Valve included or trim kit: listings marked "trim kit" need the matching rough-in valve, sold separately.
  • Handles: most include handles; a few are sold less handles, and the title says so.
  • Spout reach and height: confirm the spout reaches over the bowl.
  • Flow rate and drain: verify the flow rate limit where you install, and note whether a drain assembly is included.

Common questions

What is the difference between widespread and centerset?

A widespread faucet has a separate spout and two handles, usually 8 inches apart. A centerset puts the spout and handles on one base over 4-inch holes.

Do Moen widespread trim kits include the valve?

No. Listings marked "trim kit" need the matching Moen rough-in valve, which is sold separately.

Are the handles included?

Most are complete faucets or trim kits with handles. A few are sold less handles; the listing title says so.

Single-hole bathroom faucets from hansgrohe, Delta, Moen, Grohe, Gerber, Brizo and Pfister. A single-hole faucet mounts through one hole in the sink or countertop, usually with one handle on the faucet body. Moen models include the Align, Eva, Brantford, Gibson, Genta LX and Rizon lines; Delta lines include Trinsic, Saylor and Ashlyn; hansgrohe models include Metris and Joleena, and Gerber adds Amalfi and Lemora. Finishes include chrome, brushed nickel, oil rubbed bronze and matte black. Many models flow at 1.2 gpm, and several include a pop-up or touch-down drain, which is named in the listing title. Taller vessel faucets are made to reach over a sink that sits on top of the counter. If the sink is drilled with three holes, choose a model with an optional deck plate to cover the outer two.

How to choose

  • Hole count: confirm the sink or countertop has one faucet hole, or choose a model with a deck plate to cover three holes.
  • Spout height and reach: check both against the bowl, especially for vessel sinks.
  • Flow rate: verify the flow rate meets local requirements; many models here are 1.2 gpm.
  • Drain: note whether a drain assembly is included.
  • Supply connection: measure the distance to the supply stops for connector length.

Common questions

Can a single-hole faucet go on a three-hole sink?

Yes, with a deck plate (escutcheon) that covers the two outer holes. Some faucets include one; check the listing.

What is a vessel faucet?

A taller single-hole faucet made to reach over a vessel sink that sits on top of the counter.

What flow rate should a bathroom faucet have?

WaterSense bathroom faucets flow 1.5 gpm or less, and many models here run at 1.2 gpm.

4-inch centerset bathroom faucets from Moen, Delta, American Standard, Gerber, Matco-Norca, Pfister, Elkay, Grohe and Zurn, in two-handle and single-handle versions. A centerset faucet fits a sink with three holes drilled 4 inches apart, measured center to center between the two outer holes; the spout and handles sit on one base plate that covers all three. Residential lines include Moen Brantford, Gibson and Glyde, Delta Classic, Foundations and Woodhurst, and Gerber Antioch. Commercial models for public and institutional restrooms include Moen M-DURA and M-BITION, Delta Commercial HDF, Zurn AquaSpec and American Standard Monterrey with wrist blade handles. Flow rates run from 0.5 gpm to 1.5 gpm, and some models ship with a drain assembly. Count the holes and measure between the outer two before ordering.

How to choose

  • Hole spacing: three holes, 4" center to center between the outer two. It is not the width of the faucet.
  • One or two handles: single-handle models on a 4" base plate cover the same three-hole drilling.
  • Flow rate: 0.5 gpm for public restrooms, 1.2 gpm for most homes, 1.5 gpm at the upper end.
  • Handle type: wrist blade and lever handles suit accessible and commercial installations.
  • Drain: check whether a pop-up or touch-down drain is included.

What centerset means, and how to know you need one

A 4-inch centerset faucet fits a sink with three holes drilled 4 inches apart, center to center, measured between the two outer holes. The spout and both handles sit on one continuous base plate that covers all three. It is the most common configuration in American bathrooms and it is what almost every builder-grade vanity top is drilled for.

The two alternatives: a single-hole faucet needs one hole and one only, and a widespread faucet uses three holes spread 8 to 16 inches apart with the spout and handles as separate pieces. Count the holes and measure between the outer two before ordering - it is the one measurement that decides everything, and it takes ten seconds.

What people get wrong: the 4 inches is not the width of the faucet, and it is not the distance between the handles you can see. It is hole to hole in the deck.

Single-handle on a centerset deck

Seventeen of these are single-handle faucets built on a 4" base plate - one lever, but still covering the three-hole drilling. Delta's Classic (501-DST, 520-MPU-DST) and Foundations (B501LF, B510LF), Moen's Chateau L64621, American Standard's Colony PRO 7075000 and Reliant 3. This is the answer when you want the look of one handle without redrilling or replacing the vanity top.

Commercial, institutional and ADA handles

Eight faucets here are built for public and institutional restrooms: Moen's M-DURA (8215F12, 8413F12) and M-BITION 8915, Delta's Commercial HDF 501LF-HDF, Zurn's AquaSpec Z81104-XL-3M with a vandal-resistant pressure-compensating aerator, Elkay's LK402T4, and American Standard's Monterrey 5500170 and 7500180.

The giveaway is the handle. Wrist blade and long lever handles exist because the accessibility standard requires a faucet that can be operated without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, with no more than five pounds of force. A round knob fails that on its face; a four-inch wrist blade passes, because a forearm or a closed fist will turn it. If you are specifying for a school, clinic or public building, that is the detail the inspector looks at.

Flow rate

Four faucets here run 0.5 gpm, which is the public-restroom standard - low enough that a running tap wastes very little. Eight run 1.2 gpm, now the common residential specification and below the WaterSense threshold. Three run 1.5 gpm, the WaterSense maximum for a lavatory faucet. For a home bathroom, 1.2 gpm is the sensible default; 0.5 gpm in a residence will feel starved.

Check whether the drain is included

Twelve of these ship with a drain assembly - Gerber's touch-down and 50/50 pop-up drains, Moen's metal pop-up on the Brantford and Gibson. The rest do not. That means a second order, so compare what is in the box. The Gerber DA667229BN cover plate is the other side of the same question: it lets a single-hole faucet sit on a three-hole sink, which is how you go the other direction without a new top.

Common questions

What does 4-inch centerset mean?

The sink has three holes with 4" between the centers of the two outer holes. The faucet's spout and handles sit on one base plate that covers all three.

Can a single-handle faucet go on a centerset sink?

Yes. Single-handle faucets built on a 4" base plate cover the three-hole drilling with one lever.

Does a centerset faucet come with a drain?

Some do. Listings that include a pop-up or touch-down drain say so in the title; the rest need a drain ordered separately.

Pull-down and pull-out kitchen faucets from Moen, Delta, Gerber, Grohe, hansgrohe, Pfister, Brizo, Matco-Norca, Franke, Peerless, American Standard, Elkay and Rohl. They are single-handle faucets at 1.5 or 1.75 gpm, in polished chrome, stainless, matte black, oil rubbed bronze, champagne bronze, brushed gold and graphite. A pull-down faucet has a tall arc and a sprayer that comes straight down into the bowl. A pull-out faucet has a lower spout and a sprayer that comes toward you, which suits a sink under a window or a low upper cabinet. Moen models include Align, Brantford, Sleek and Camerist, with Reflex docking and Power Clean or Power Boost spray; Gerber uses SnapBack retraction; Grohe Concetto and Delta Emmeline are also listed. Spray patterns run from a single stream to dual and triple spray.

How to choose

  • Arc and clearance: measure from the deck to whatever is above it. A pull-down needs headroom; a pull-out fits under a window or low cabinet.
  • Hole count: a single-handle faucet needs one hole. On a three-hole sink, add a deck plate if one is not in the box.
  • Flow rate: the federal maximum for a kitchen faucet is 2.2 gpm and several states set a lower limit; faucets here are 1.5 or 1.75 gpm.
  • Finish: stainless-look finishes have different names by brand and do not match each other exactly.
  • Spout reach: compare the reach with the bowl position, especially on double-bowl sinks.

Pull-down and pull-out faucets in detail

Pull-down or pull-out is decided by the sink and the wall behind it, not by the faucet. A pull-down has a tall arc and the sprayer comes straight down into the bowl — it wants headroom, and it is the right answer over a deep single-bowl sink. A pull-out has a lower spout and the sprayer comes toward you, which is what works under a window, beneath a low upper cabinet, or on a shallow or double-bowl sink where a high arc would just splash. The pull-out also reaches further onto the counter, which matters if you fill pots off the sink rather than in it. Measure the clearance from the deck to whatever is above it before choosing the arc.

The retraction system is the part that fails, and every brand solves it differently. Moen's Reflex and Gerber's SnapBack both use a counterweight on the hose to pull the sprayer back and hold it docked; Moen's Power Clean and Power Boost are spray-force features, not docking ones. When a sprayer sags out of the spout or will not seat, the cause is almost always under the sink and not in the head: the counterweight has slid along the hose, or the hose is snagged on a shutoff, a disposal or the trap. Reseat the weight at the manufacturer's spacing and clear the hose path before replacing anything.

A single-handle faucet needs one hole, and most sinks are drilled for three. That gap is what the deck plate covers, and it is the part people leave off the order and then discover on installation day. Some faucets here ship with one — Gerber's G0040164 Viper names it in the box — and for the rest it is a separate line item. Check the sink's hole count and spacing before ordering, because a three-hole sink with a one-hole faucet and no deck plate cannot be finished.

Flow is capped by law: the federal maximum for a kitchen faucet is 2.2 gpm, and several states set a lower limit. Nothing here exceeds 1.75 gpm and the Grohe Concetto and several Delta and American Standard models run 1.5, so the stock clears the stricter state caps as well as the federal one.

Five brands, five names for the same silver finish. Moen calls it Spot Resist Stainless, Delta calls it Arctic Stainless, Grohe calls it SuperSteel, Hansgrohe calls it Stainless Steel Optic and Franke calls it Stainless Steel. They photograph almost identically and they do not match each other across a kitchen. If the sink, the faucet and the disposal air switch come from three brands, pick the finish family once and accept that only one of them will be exact.

Spray patterns run from a single stream to dual and triple spray, and spout reach from a 14" prep faucet to a 17.5" high-arc. Bar and prep sinks have their own shorter line in pull-out prep and bar faucets; replacement sprayers and hoses are in faucet parts.

Common questions

What is the difference between a pull-down and a pull-out faucet?

A pull-down has a tall arc and the sprayer comes straight down into the bowl. A pull-out has a lower spout and the sprayer comes toward you, which works under a window or a low upper cabinet.

Will a single-handle kitchen faucet fit a three-hole sink?

Yes, with a deck plate that covers the two unused holes. Some faucets include one; for the rest it is a separate item, so check the listing.

Why does my pull-down sprayer not retract?

The cause is usually under the sink: the counterweight has slid along the hose, or the hose is caught on a shutoff, the disposal or the trap. Reseat the weight at the manufacturer's spacing and clear the hose path.

Tub and shower trim kits: the handle, escutcheon, tub spout and showerhead that mount on the finished wall over a rough-in valve. Brands include Moen, Delta, Pfister and Gerber. Moen kits cover the Posi-Temp and M-CORE valve families in the Align, Brantford, Eva, Genta LX, Gibson, Glyde, Rizon and Voss lines. Delta kits are listed by Monitor series, and Gerber kits name the Treysta valve they fit. Pfister two-handle and three-handle tub and shower faucets are also here. Finishes are chrome, matte black, brushed nickel, stainless and oil-rubbed bronze. Trim is bought separately from the valve body and only fits the valve family it was designed for: a Moen trim will not fit a Delta rough-in, and within a brand the cartridge generation matters. Kits marked "no head" or "NH" leave out the showerhead.

How to choose

  • Valve compatibility: identify the valve in the wall before ordering. Trim for a current valve often will not seat on a fifteen-year-old body, even from the same brand.
  • What is included: most kits have the handle, escutcheon, tub spout and showerhead. The title says if the showerhead is left out or if a valve is included.
  • Escutcheon coverage: on a retrofit, a smaller plate can expose unfinished tile that the old one hid. Compare plate sizes.
  • Finish: oil-rubbed bronze is a living finish on some lines and changes with handling, so pieces bought years apart may not match.
  • Diverter: the tub spout diverter switches between tub and shower. Adding a hand shower or body sprays takes a separate in-wall valve.

Common questions

What comes in a tub and shower trim kit?

Usually the handle, the escutcheon plate, the tub spout and the showerhead. Kits marked "no head" or "NH" leave out the showerhead, and every kit leaves out the rough-in valve.

How do I know which trim kit fits my valve?

Match the brand and valve family. For Moen, a Posi-Temp valve takes Posi-Temp trim and an M-CORE valve takes M-CORE trim of the same series.

What is the difference between a tub/shower trim and a shower-only trim?

A tub/shower kit includes a tub spout with a diverter. A shower-only kit has just the handle, escutcheon and showerhead.

Shower trim kits from Moen, Delta, Pfister, Gerber and Grohe: the handle, escutcheon and showerhead that finish a stand-up shower. A trim set is not a valve. It is the visible half of the assembly, and behind the wall it needs a rough-in valve body, sold separately unless the listing says the valve is included. Trim only fits its own manufacturer's valve family: Moen trim goes on the matching Moen Posi-Temp or M-CORE valve, and Delta trim goes on the Delta MultiChoice rough-in. Finishes are led by chrome, brushed nickel and matte black. Many sets are 1.75 GPM and carry WaterSense, and many are listed ADA compliant, which on a trim set refers to lever handle operation. If the showerhead is staying and only the handle is being replaced, a valve-only trim is the simpler part.

How to choose

  • Valve compatibility: confirm which rough-in is in the wall. On a remodel it cannot be checked after the tile is up.
  • Flow rate: several states cap shower flow below the federal 2.5 GPM, including California, Colorado, New York and Washington. Check the GPM in the listing.
  • Finish name: brushed nickel, spot resist brushed nickel and stainless are three different finishes. Order the room from one finish name.
  • Handle: lever handles operate without tight grasping, pinching or twisting, which is what an ADA listing on trim refers to.
  • Outlets: a shower with more than one outlet needs an in-wall diverter or transfer valve.

Common questions

Does a shower trim kit include the valve?

No. A trim kit is the handle, escutcheon and showerhead. The rough-in valve in the wall is sold separately, and the trim must match its brand and valve family.

What does "shower only" mean on a Moen trim?

It means the kit has no tub spout. It is for a stand-up shower; for a tub and shower combination, see tub-shower trim sets.

Can I replace only the shower handle?

Yes. If the showerhead is staying, a valve-only trim with just the handle and escutcheon is the simpler part.

Thermostatic shower valve trim from hansgrohe, Grohe and Brizo, with one TOTO Keane trim. A thermostatic valve holds the outlet temperature at the setting you choose, and the trim is the visible handle and plate that mounts over it. hansgrohe trims include Ecostat S, Ecostat E, Ecostat Square, Ecostat Classic and Locarno with volume control, with or without a diverter, and ShowerSelect S for two functions. Grohe trims are listed as single, dual and triple function, along with an extension kit for SmartControl trims and Grohe thermostatic shower systems. Brizo trims include Invari, Vettis and Litze TempAssure, some with a diverter or supplied less handles. Finishes include chrome, brushed nickel, matte black, polished nickel, Luxe Gold and Grohe Hard Graphite. Thermostatic trim works only with the matching rough-in valve from the same manufacturer and series.

How to choose

  • Valve compatibility: confirm the valve body in the wall, by manufacturer and series, before ordering the trim.
  • Functions: check how many outlets the trim controls: single, dual or triple function, or volume control with a diverter.
  • Handles: some Brizo trims are supplied less handles; the handle kit is a separate item.
  • Wall depth: note the wall depth range of the valve and whether an extension kit is needed for thicker walls.
  • Finish: finish names are specific to each brand, so match the other fittings in the room by name.

Common questions

Does thermostatic trim include the valve?

Listings named "trim" are the visible parts only. The thermostatic rough-in valve is ordered separately and must be the matching valve from the same manufacturer and series.

What is the difference between thermostatic and pressure-balance trim?

A pressure-balance valve holds the hot and cold mix steady when pressure changes. A thermostatic valve holds the outlet temperature itself, which is the usual choice for showers with several outlets. Each takes its own trim.

What does "with volume control and diverter" mean?

The trim has a temperature handle plus a control for water volume, and a diverter that sends water to one outlet or another, such as a showerhead and a hand shower.

Shower and tub-shower rough-in valves: the valve body that goes in the wall before it closes, in pressure-balance, thermostatic and multi-outlet configurations. Brands include Moen, Delta, Grohe, Brizo, Rohl, American Standard and DXV. Moen M-PACT Posi-Temp and M-CORE valves are listed by connection type; Delta and Brizo MultiChoice Universal rough-ins, Grohe pressure balance rough-ins and the American Standard and DXV Flash rough-in are also here. The rough-in and the finish trim are two separate purchases, so the valve can be set during construction and the finish chosen later. The two must belong to the same manufacturer family: a Moen trim will not fit a Delta body, and cartridge families change between generations within a brand. A pressure-balance valve holds the hot-cold ratio when pressure drops elsewhere; a thermostatic valve holds the outlet temperature.

How to choose

  • Valve family: choose the valve for the trim you want. Trim and valve must come from the same manufacturer family.
  • Pressure-balance or thermostatic: pressure-balance suits a single-outlet shower or tub-shower; thermostatic is what a multi-outlet shower needs.
  • Connection type: sweat (CC) for copper, IPS for threaded pipe, or crimp ring or cold-expansion PEX. Universal bodies accept more than one.
  • Integral stops: check whether the body includes stops. Without them, servicing the cartridge means shutting off the whole house.
  • Outlets: a tub-shower body has two outlets; more outlets need a diverter or transfer valve.

Shower valve replacement

If a shower drips, runs too hot or too cold, or the handle is stiff, the fix is usually the cartridge, not the whole valve. Replace the valve body when it is corroded, leaking inside the wall, or not pressure-balanced. Staying with the same brand and valve family keeps your trim options open and can limit how much tile you need to open. Find cartridges in tub and shower repair parts, and match the finish with shower trim sets, tub-shower trim sets or thermostatic valve trims.

Common questions

What is a rough-in shower valve?

It is the valve body that is plumbed into the wall before the tile goes up. The handle and escutcheon (the trim) are bought separately and mount over it.

Pressure-balance or thermostatic: which do I need?

Pressure-balance valves keep the hot and cold mix steady when pressure changes and meet code in most homes. Thermostatic valves hold a set temperature and are the usual choice for showers with several outlets.

Which connection type should I choose?

Pick the inlet that matches your supply pipe: sweat (CC) for copper, IPS for threaded pipe, or crimp ring or cold-expansion PEX. Many Moen M-PACT and M-CORE valves are listed by connection type in the title.

Moen shower trim, rough-in valves, bathroom and kitchen faucets, Roman tub trim, shower heads and body sprays, plus Moen bath accessories and replacement parts. Most of the range is shower and tub-shower trim for the Posi-Temp and M-CORE valve families, along with the M-PACT and M-CORE rough-in valves and transfer valves they mount on. The model number on each trim names its collection: Align, Brantford, Eva, Gibson, Genta LX, Glyde, Voss, Rizon, Cia, Doux and others, so a matching faucet, tub spout and shower trim can be chosen from one line and one finish. Kitchen faucets include the Arbor, Align, Sleek, Genta LX, Method and Camerist pull-down and pull-out models, some with Reflex docking, Power Clean spray or MotionSense touchless control. Finishes include chrome, Spot Resist stainless, brushed nickel, matte black, oil rubbed bronze and brushed gold.

How to choose

  • Order the trim by the valve in the wall: Posi-Temp trim fits a Posi-Temp rough-in, M-CORE 2-Series and 3-Series trim fits its own M-CORE valve, and Moentrol trim fits a Moentrol body.
  • Valve included or not: trim kits are the visible parts. Each listing title says whether the valve is included or sold separately.
  • Connection type: M-PACT and M-CORE rough-in valves are listed by inlet: CC (sweat), IPS, crimp ring PEX or cold-expansion PEX.
  • Finish: choose one finish name for the room; Spot Resist stainless and brushed nickel are different finishes.
  • Changing the look later: trim made for the valve already installed can be swapped from the finished wall without opening it.

Common questions

Which Moen valve do I have?

Remove the handle and look at the cartridge. A Posi-Temp valve uses a 1222 cartridge, an M-CORE 2-Series valve uses a 1212 cartridge, an M-CORE 3-Series valve uses a 1213 cartridge, and a Moentrol valve uses a 1225 cartridge. Choose trim made for that valve family.

Is the valve included with Moen trim kits?

No. Moen trim kits are the visible parts: handle, escutcheon and, where listed, the showerhead and tub spout. The rough-in valve is sold separately, and each listing says so in its title.

What does Posi-Temp mean?

Posi-Temp is Moen's pressure-balancing valve. It keeps the hot and cold mix steady when water pressure changes elsewhere in the house, such as when a toilet flushes.

American Standard fixtures and parts: toilet bowls and tanks sold separately, wall-mount and pedestal sinks, bathroom and kitchen faucets, shower valves and repair components, split between commercial-grade and residential products. Toilet lines include Cadet PRO, Colony, Champion and Edgemere, with wall-hung Glenwall and Afwall bowls for commercial work. Bowls and tanks are listed as separate items on two-piece toilets, so a cracked tank does not mean a new toilet, but the tank has to match the bowl model, since bolt spacing and the flush valve opening vary across the line. Repair parts include flappers, flush valves, tank-to-bowl coupling kits, trip levers and pressure balance cartridges. Faucets include Colony PRO and Monterrey, and shower rough-ins include the Flash valve. Finishes are mostly white, with linen and biscuit as the off-white options and chrome and brushed nickel on trim.

How to choose

  • Bowl and tank match: bowls and tanks are not universally interchangeable. Match the tank to the bowl model.
  • Rough-in: the distance from the finished wall to the closet bolt centerline. 12" is standard; 10" and 14" appear in older construction.
  • Flush valve size: match the flapper or seal to the flush valve opening, commonly 2" or 3"; Champion models use a larger flush valve with its own seal.
  • Color: American Standard white and another manufacturer's white are close but not identical, which shows when brands are mixed.
  • Shower cartridge: match the cartridge to the valve in the wall, not to the trim.

Common questions

How do I find American Standard toilet parts for my toilet?

Look for the model number stamped inside the tank, usually on the back wall above the water line. Flappers, flush valves and tank-to-bowl kits are matched to the model. See toilet repair parts.

Which flapper fits my American Standard toilet?

Match the size of the flush valve opening in the tank, commonly 2" or 3". Champion models use a larger flush valve with its own tank seal, such as the 738659-0070A Champion Tank Seal.

Which cartridge fits my American Standard shower valve?

Match the cartridge to the valve in the wall, not to the trim. Use the valve model number from the installation paperwork or compare the old cartridge, then order the listed replacement.
